topic.title: We read 1-star reviews to buy
topic.claim: We read 1-star reviews to decide to buy, not to avoid. If the complaint is about delivery, we're sold.
topic.moment: You skip the 5 stars and go straight to the angriest review, which says 'box came dented'.

turn.actually: Bad reviews are the only ones we trust, so a harmless complaint works as an endorsement.

topic.feeling: Relieved I finally have a reason to trust something.
topic.villain: Review sections so full of paid praise that only complaints feel real
topic.because: We know 5-star reviews can be bought. A real complaint about a small thing proves the product survived real use.
topic.payoff: The best review a brand can get is a 1-star about the courier.
topic.behaviour: Shoppers filter by lowest rating first and buy if the flaws are irrelevant to them.
topic.mechanism: Paid praise made complaints the only signal left.
topic.group: Online shoppers who research before buying
topic.send_to: The friend who takes 40 minutes to buy a kettle
topic.why_now: Paid and fake reviews have made star ratings feel useless.

score.why: We go straight to the angriest review, and a harmless complaint ends up working as an endorsement. It's a funny, true habit most people never examine.

notes: slide 5-6: These two slides re-explain what slide 4 already landed. "So praise stopped meaning anything. Anyone with a budget can buy it" repeats slide 4, and "Online, you can't pick the kettle up" tells readers something they already know. Merge them into one slide. Keep "no brand pays a stranger to complain" and "a stranger's bad mood is the closest you get" and cut the rest. Drop the "Isn't that a bit paranoid?" beat, because nobody was asking it.

slide 6: "Someone angry enough to write a paragraph actually used the thing. The worst they found was the box." doesn't hold up. A dented-box reviewer may never have used the kettle. Rephrase the logic: if the loudest complaint on the page is about the box, then nothing inside gave them a reason to complain. That is the real reason a harmless complaint works as an endorsement, and it is the turn the topic promises.

slide 3: This is three "Fine." examples in a row, and the third adds nothing new. Cut to two. Use the space for the contrast that makes it feel insider: the same 1-star hunt kills the kettle when the angriest review says "stopped heating in 2 days". That shows readers they are filtering for what they can live with, not for the lowest star count. It also shows how the filter actually works.

sources.fact: A LocalCircles survey found 46% of Indian e-commerce users always check ratings and reviews before buying, 56% found ratings positively biased, and only 16% believe their negative reviews were consistently published. It does not show that shoppers sort by lowest rating or buy when a complaint concerns delivery.
sources.excerpt: Nearly 56 percent of online shoppers found ratings on eCommerce sites and apps to be positively biased | 46 percent of eCommerce users always referred to ratings and reviews when making purchases | Additionally, just 16 percent of consumers believe that their negative reviews were consistently published in the past year.

sources.fact: The Department of Consumer Affairs launched IS 19000:2022, a framework on online consumer reviews that was voluntary at launch, because shoppers cannot inspect products online and so need genuine reviews.
sources.excerpt: The standards will be applicable to every online platform which publishes consumer reviews. | The standard will initially be voluntary for compliance by all e-commerce platforms. | violation of the standards by any entity may be considered as an unfair trade practice or violation of consumer rights | it is essential that reviews are genuine and authentic.

cover.headline: We read [1-star reviews] to buy, not to avoid
cover.sub: The angriest review on the page is the one we trust.

paragraphs: We don't read 1-star reviews to avoid a product. We read them to buy it.
slides.why_swipe: Why would a bad review make anyone buy?

paragraphs: You're buying a ₹1,800 kettle. 4.3 stars. It's midnight and the cart is already open.
Your thumb flies past the wall of 5-star reviews like it's an ad.
slides.why_swipe: So where does the thumb stop?

paragraphs: You tap "1 star" first and hunt for the angriest person on the page.
"Box came dented." Fine. You add it to cart.
Mixer grinder? "Colour different from photo." Earphones? "Delivery took 6 days." Same verdict.
But if the angriest review on that same kettle says "stopped heating in 2 days", the tab is closed. Stars were never the test. Can you live with the flaw? That's it.
slides.why_swipe: Why do we skip the good reviews?

paragraphs: Because we know how 5 stars get made.
The card in the box begging for 5 stars. The seller's call to check you're happy, right before asking for a rating.
The "superb product, value for money" posted the day it arrived, before the kettle boiled anything.
slides.why_swipe: And it's not just a hunch.

paragraphs: 56% of Indian online shoppers found ratings positively biased.
So when an angry review makes it through, we read it like a leaked document.
slides.why_swipe: So what are we actually reading in it?

paragraphs: A bad review is a stranger holding the kettle so you don't have to.
If a dented box is the worst anyone found, the kettle is fine.
slides.why_swipe: So what does the perfect review look like?

paragraphs: The best review a brand can get is a 1-star about the courier.
"Product is good but delivery boy didn't come upstairs. Very disappointed."

end.save: Come back to this on your next midnight scroll through the lowest ratings.
end.send: Send to the friend who takes 40 minutes to buy a kettle.

draft.caption: What's the most harmless 1-star review that made you hit buy?
draft.alt_text: A nine-slide text post arguing that Indian shoppers read 1-star reviews to decide to buy, not to avoid. At midnight, the shopper skips the 5-star reviews and hunts for the angriest one. If the complaint is a dented box, a wrong colour or slow delivery, they buy. If it says the kettle stopped heating, the tab closes. Because 5-star reviews feel bought, and 56% of Indian online shoppers found ratings positively biased, an angry review reads like a leaked document. A bad review is a stranger holding the kettle for you, and if a dented box is the worst anyone found, the kettle is fine. It ends: the best review a brand can get is a 1-star about the courier.

claims.text: 56% of Indian online shoppers found ratings positively biased.
